analysis.one_liner: Requires cell phone carriers to warn users before overage charges and get consent first.
analysis.headline: The bill was never taken up: introduced in late September 2010 with no cosponsors, it was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and died when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the FCC to write rules telling cell phone companies to alert customers when they hit 80% of their monthly minutes, texts, or data, and to get the customer's okay before allowing — and charging for — anything beyond the plan. The alerts and the customer's consent could not themselves count against the plan or cost extra. An FCC survey cited in the bill found 1 in 6 mobile customers had experienced 'bill shock,' a sudden bill spike with no change to their plan.
analysis.who_benefits: Cell phone subscribers, especially those on capped or prepaid plans, who would get a free warning before racking up overage charges on minutes, texts, or data, and whose plans could not be exceeded without their say-so. The warning itself could not eat into their plan's allowance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Cell phone customers on capped plans

how_it_helps.text: Carriers would have to notify a subscriber free of charge — by voice message, text, or email — when they have used 80% of their monthly limit of minutes, texts, or data, and the notice could not count against the plan. [S2] [S3]

Carriers could not allow services beyond the monthly limit without the subscriber's consent, given free of charge and not counted against the plan, so overage charges would only happen if the customer knowingly agreed. [S2] [S3]

The bill's findings cite an FCC survey finding that 1 in 6 mobile subscribers had experienced 'bill shock,' and that most of those customers got no warning before exceeding their limits or seeing their bill spike. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Wireless carriers, which would have to build notification and consent systems and forgo revenue from customers who silently exceed their plan limits and get billed for overages.

drawbacks.text: Carriers would bear the cost of building and running the notification and consent systems, and would lose overage-fee revenue from customers who today exceed their limits without realizing it; some of that cost could show up in plan prices. [S2] [S3]

Requiring consent before any overage use could cut off a customer mid-task — for example, stop data service on a road trip — until they respond to the alert, an inconvenience for people who would happily pay for the extra usage. [S3]
The bill delegates the details to FCC rulemaking rather than writing the consumer protections into law, so the strength of the safeguards would depend on how the agency drafted the rules. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the benefit is straightforward: a free warning before an overage and no surprise charges without consent, ending a billing practice the FCC itself had flagged as widespread. The costs fall mainly on carriers, and the main consumer downside is a possible speed bump for people who want to exceed their plan on purpose. The design is simple and the trade-off weighs clearly toward the customer.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Udall introduced the Cell Phone Bill Shock Act of 2010 on September 29, 2010, near the end of the 111th Congress. [S1] [S5]
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation; that was the last action on the bill. [S5]
No senator cosponsored the bill, and no committee markup, floor vote, or further consideration is recorded before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011. [S4] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wireless carriers came out ahead: with the bill never reaching a vote, nothing required them to warn customers before overage charges or obtain consent, and billing for plan overruns could continue as before. Customers who hit their plan limits without a warning kept bearing the surprise charges the bill was written to stop.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wireless carriers kept the status quo

for.name: Sen. Tom Udall
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Mexico (bill sponsor)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor; secured no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred (chair at the time: Sen. Jay Rockefeller, D-WV)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on September 29, 2010 and took no further action on it; it never received a markup or a vote.

against.name: Wireless carriers
against.what_they_did: Had a direct financial stake in the outcome, since the bill would have curtailed billing customers for usage beyond their plan limits without notice or consent; no position by the industry is recorded in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no senator besides the sponsor signed on, so there is no record of where either party stood; the bill simply died in committee.

industries.note: The bill would have required free alerts at 80% of a customer's plan limits and consent before any overage use, cutting into revenue from overage fees charged to customers who exceeded their plans without realizing it. A carrier's interest in continuing silent overage billing ran directly against the customer's interest in knowing before being charged. [S2] [S3]
